Hi Phil,

I hope I could get some advice from you.

I have a clinical survey data where a single item have two responses. There are 24 items in total. The former response (binary) influences the latter responses (polytomous) to some degree.  On top of that, the content of the items are theoretically distinct (i.e. two factors: doing things on your own, doing things with others).

For example,
Walk down the street on your own. (18 items - F1)
Walk down the street with your friends. (9 items - F2)
The responses to these questions are the following:
Do you feel you could do this right now (Yes/No)
How anxious would you feel doing this? (0 - No distress, 5 - moderate distress, 10 - extremely distress).

In some cases, someone might feel anxious doing it (Yes), and have moderate distress (5). In other cases someone might not feel anxious doing it (0), but, they may also have moderate distress (5). The general correlation is that someone who is anxious will also feel distress and vice versa, though the correlation is not 1. This tells me that there is some sort of individual differences at work.

My question is how best should I model such data under the mirt framework? My instinct would be to try multi-level mirt using the mixedmirt(), but most examples are based on person grouping variable rather than item grouping variable. I read through this thread (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!newtopic/mirt-package/mirt-package/gN0JeJVHoQA) as well, but the grouping variable was on the persons side. I was hoping that you could give some advice on how best I can use the mixedmirt() framework to model this type of data.

Thanks!
Aiden

> Totally agree with your `The distribution of sum scores is not synonymous with the distribution of the latent traits`.  But they are highly correlated.

I'm still not sure why exactly you believe this to be true, but it's demonstrably false. For instance, you can have a strong positive skewness in the sum-scores and yet the latent trait scores are genuinely normal. See the code and figures below. This is why I'm still not sure why you think your latent traits are non-normal based only on total score information.

library(mirt)
set.seed(1234)
a <- rlnorm(50, .2, .2)
d <- -rlnorm(50, .2, .4)
theta <- matrix(rnorm(5000))

dat <- simdata(a, d, itemtype = '2PL', Theta=theta)
hist(rowSums(dat), 20, main = 'Histogram of total scores')

mod <- mirt(dat, 1)
coef(mod, simplify=TRUE)
fs <- fscores(mod, method = 'plausible')
hist(fs, 30, main = 'Histogram of plausible latent trait estimates')

> If sub-groups' latent distribution is not normal,can I still use `dentype = "Gaussian"`? If not,what  alternative dentype can use?

If you must, and believe that your latent traits are indeed non-normal, you could try to fit mixture or Davidian curves as potential semi-parametric smoothing solutions. Or, if you have a more specific distributional form, simply write your own using createGroup() as I've stated in previous posts.

messages.subject: Re: How does mirt function manage missing data ?
messages.subject_clean: How does mirt function manage missing data ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sherry,

mirt primarily uses the MML framework outlined by Bock and Atikin(1981). Your description of the algorithm is effectively correct for missing data w.r.t. calculating the marginal probabilities. The E-step doesn't really change when missing data are present, it just affects the marginal probabilities where the prior distribution becomes more important for cases with less information (i.e., the likelihood component becomes less impactful since less information is present for these individuals). See below for a demonstration of this.

library(mirt)
dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)
mod <- mirt(dat, 1, technical = list(storeEtable=TRUE))
Etable <- mod@Internals$Etable[[1]]$r1
Etable

apply(dat, 2, table)
matrix(colSums(Etable), nrow=2)

dat2 <- dat
dat2[1,1] <- NA
mod <- mirt(dat2, 1, technical = list(storeEtable=TRUE))
Etable <- mod@Internals$Etable[[1]]$r1
Etable

apply(dat2, 2, table)
matrix(colSums(Etable), nrow=2)

Phil

messages.subject: Re: If some sub-group are not normal distribution,can I use multipleGroup()?
messages.subject_clean: If some sub-group are not normal distribution,can I use multipleGroup()?
messages.body_plain:
If you're not sure of the latent trait distribution then I'm not sure it makes sense to play around with different prior distributions. Just treat the latent trait distribution as an initial prior, where you know the results could be biased (this is a typical Bayesian mentality). You could use fscores() to approximate some distribution after the fact, but again this is only approximate since a) the model is likely biased from choosing an incorrect latent trait distribution prior, and b) the prior used in many  the point-wise computations of the latent traits is also likely incorrect, leading to a double amount of noise. Latent traits are tricky at times, and two-step approaches are not perfect.

Phil

mixedmirt fits MIRT models using FIML estimation to dichotomous and polytomous IRT models conditional on fixed and random effect of person and item level covariates.
